subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry, Units 1 and 2
about: VCE, Materials, water, acids and measuring chemicals
syllabus: VCE Chemistry Study Design (from 2023), Units 1 and 2

units.title: Unit 1: How can the diversity of materials be explained?

points.title: Atomic structure
points.brief: Atoms have protons, neutrons and electrons. Atomic number, mass number and charge identify an element, isotope or ion.

points.title: Electron configuration
points.brief: Electrons fill shells and subshells (s, p, d) in a set order, which explains an element's place in the periodic table.

points.title: The periodic table's layout
points.brief: Elements are arranged by atomic number into groups (columns) with similar properties and periods (rows).

points.title: Periodic trends
points.brief: Across a period, atomic radius falls and electronegativity and first ionisation energy rise. Down a group the reverse.

points.title: Critical elements
points.brief: Elements such as helium, phosphorus and the rare-earth metals are scarce but needed for technology, so recovering them by recycling matters.

points.title: Covalent bonding
points.brief: Non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons to form molecules or networks.

points.title: Lewis structures
points.brief: Diagrams showing bonding pairs and lone pairs of valence electrons in a molecule.

points.title: Molecular shapes
points.brief: Electron pairs repel to sit as far apart as possible, giving shapes such as linear, bent, pyramidal and tetrahedral.

points.title: Polarity of bonds and molecules
points.brief: A bond is polar when atoms differ in electronegativity. A molecule is polar if its shape leaves the charges uneven.

points.title: Intermolecular forces
points.brief: Dispersion forces act between all molecules, dipole-dipole forces between polar ones, and hydrogen bonds where H bonds to N, O or F.

points.title: Properties of molecular substances
points.brief: Weak forces between molecules give low melting and boiling points, and molecules do not conduct electricity.

points.title: Diamond and graphite
points.brief: Diamond and graphite are carbon networks. Diamond is very hard; graphite is soft and conducts because of delocalised electrons. Each suits different uses.

points.title: Metallic bonding
points.brief: Metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons explain lustre, malleability, high melting points and conduction of heat and electricity.

points.title: Reactivity of metals
points.brief: How readily metals react with water, acids and oxygen, found by experiment, gives a reactivity series.

points.title: Metal recycling
points.brief: Recycling metals into new products is an example of a circular economy, saving ore and energy.

points.title: Ionic bonding
points.brief: Metals give electrons to non-metals, forming ions held in a lattice by electrostatic attraction.

points.title: Properties of ionic compounds
points.brief: Ionic compounds have high melting points, are brittle and conduct only when molten or dissolved.

points.title: Writing ionic formulas
points.brief: Balancing ion charges gives the formula and name of an ionic compound, including those with polyatomic ions such as sulfate and nitrate.

points.title: Predicting precipitates
points.brief: Solubility tables predict when two solutions form an insoluble solid, shown in full and ionic equations with states.

points.title: Like dissolves like
points.brief: Polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents such as water, and non-polar solutes in non-polar solvents.

points.title: Chromatography
points.brief: Components of a mixture travel different distances through a stationary phase, which shows what a sample contains and how pure it is.

points.title: Rf values
points.brief: The distance a spot travels divided by the distance the solvent travels gives an Rf value that helps identify a substance.

points.title: Isotopes and relative atomic mass
points.brief: Relative isotopic masses are set against carbon-12. Mass spectrometry gives the abundance of each isotope, from which relative atomic mass is found.

points.title: The mole
points.brief: One mole is 6.02 × 10²³ particles. n = m/M links mass to amount.

points.title: Molar mass and percentage composition
points.brief: The molar mass of a compound is the sum of its atoms' masses, and gives the percentage by mass of each element.

points.title: Empirical and molecular formulas
points.brief: Percentage composition gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the molar mass then gives the actual formula.

points.title: Families of organic compounds
points.brief: Alkanes, alkenes, haloalkanes, alcohols and carboxylic acids each share a general formula and similar properties.

points.title: Structural and semi-structural formulas
points.brief: Structural and semi-structural formulas show how atoms are joined, including the functional group that sets each family apart.

points.title: Naming simple organic compounds
points.brief: IUPAC names show the chain length, the bonds and any functional group, such as but-2-ene.

points.title: Organic chemicals from plants
points.brief: Plant biomass can replace oil as a renewable source of solvents, medicines, adhesives, dyes and paints.

points.title: Organic materials in everyday life
points.brief: Fabrics, foods, medicines, cosmetics, pesticides and car parts are all made from organic compounds.

points.title: Addition and condensation polymers
points.brief: Addition polymers join monomers with double bonds and nothing lost. Condensation polymers join monomers and release a small molecule such as water.

points.title: Addition polymers
points.brief: Alkene monomers join by opening their double bonds into long chains, such as ethene into polyethene.

points.title: Thermoplastics and thermosets
points.brief: Thermoplastics soften when heated because chains are not cross-linked. Thermosets are cross-linked and do not.

points.title: Designing polymers
points.brief: Choosing the monomer, chain length and amount of branching gives a plastic the properties a use needs.

points.title: Fossil plastics and bioplastics
points.brief: Plastics such as PVC and polystyrene come from oil; bioplastics such as PLA come from plants. Each can be recycled or composted in different ways.

points.title: Linear and circular economies for plastics
points.brief: Recycling, condensation polymers that break down by hydrolysis and better design move plastics from make, use and throw away towards reuse.

points.title: Primary and secondary data
points.brief: Primary data is collected first-hand; secondary data comes from others' work and must be judged for quality.

points.title: Evidence, opinion and anecdote
points.brief: Scientific evidence is tested and repeatable. Opinion and anecdote are not, so they cannot settle a scientific question.

points.title: Quality of evidence
points.brief: Good evidence is valid, comes from an authoritative source and has its possible errors and bias considered.

points.title: Green chemistry and sustainable development
points.brief: Principles such as less waste, safer chemicals and renewable feedstocks help chemistry meet needs now without harming later generations.

units.title: Unit 2: How do chemical reactions shape the natural world?

points.title: Water on Earth
points.brief: Water exists as solid, liquid and gas at Earth's surface, but only a small share is fresh water fit to drink.

points.title: Water's unusual properties
points.brief: Hydrogen bonding gives water a higher boiling point than other Group 16 hydrides and makes ice less dense than liquid water.

points.title: Specific heat capacity
points.brief: The energy to raise 1 g of a substance by 1 °C. Water's is high, so it warms and cools slowly.

points.title: Latent heat of vaporisation
points.brief: Water takes a lot of energy to evaporate, which helps keep oceans and living things at steady temperatures.

points.title: Brønsted-Lowry acids and bases
points.brief: Acids donate protons and bases accept them. Polyprotic acids can donate more than one proton.

points.title: Strong and weak acids
points.brief: Strong acids and bases ionise fully in water; weak ones only partly. Strength is not the same as concentration.

points.title: Amphiprotic substances
points.brief: Substances such as water and HCO₃⁻ can act as an acid or a base.

points.title: Neutralisation
points.brief: Acids react with hydroxides and carbonates to form salts and water. Antacids neutralise excess stomach acid.

points.title: The pH scale
points.brief: pH is a logarithmic scale of hydrogen ion concentration. The ionic product of water gives the pH of strong acid and base solutions.

points.title: Indicators and pH meters
points.brief: Natural indicators, commercial indicators and pH meters differ in accuracy and precision when measuring acidity.

points.title: Acid rain and ocean acidity
points.brief: Dissolved carbon dioxide makes rain naturally slightly acidic. Acid rain from pollution is stronger, and more carbon dioxide is making oceans less basic.

points.title: Oxidation and reduction
points.brief: Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain. Half-equations, balanced in acidic conditions, show each side of the reaction.

points.title: Metal displacement reactions
points.brief: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from solution, as the reactivity series predicts.

points.title: Corrosion and simple cells
points.brief: Rusting is a redox reaction, and simple primary cells use redox to turn chemical energy into electrical energy.

points.title: Concentration
points.brief: Concentration is solute per amount of solution, in mol/L, g/L, %(m/v), %(v/v) or ppm, with conversions between them.

points.title: Solubility
points.brief: Solubility tables and graphs show how much of a substance dissolves, and how temperature changes the solubility of solids and gases.

points.title: Removing impurities from water
points.brief: Adding a chemical that forms a precipitate with an unwanted ion removes it from water.

points.title: Volumetric analysis
points.brief: Titration with a standard solution and an indicator finds an unknown concentration, using dilution and volume-volume stoichiometry.

points.title: Greenhouse gases
points.brief: Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour absorb infrared radiation and warm the atmosphere.

points.title: Gas pressure and standard conditions
points.brief: Gas pressure is force on an area. Standard laboratory conditions are 25 °C and 100 kPa.

points.title: The ideal gas equation
points.brief: pV = nRT links pressure, volume, amount and temperature of a gas, with care over units.

points.title: Stoichiometry with gases
points.brief: Mole ratios from an equation find the mass, amount or volume of a gas made or used in a reaction.

points.title: Salts in water and soil
points.brief: Minerals and heavy metals get into water and soil. Electrical conductivity measures how salty a sample is.

points.title: Water of crystallisation
points.brief: Heating a hydrated salt drives off water, and the mass lost gives the ratio of water to salt.

points.title: Mass-mass stoichiometry
points.brief: Mole ratios from a balanced equation find the mass of one substance from the mass of another.

points.title: Colorimetry and UV-visible spectroscopy
points.brief: The amount of light a coloured solution absorbs, read against a calibration curve, gives its concentration.

points.title: Aims, hypotheses, models and theories
points.brief: An aim states what is investigated, a hypothesis predicts a result, and models, theories and laws explain or describe patterns.

points.title: Accuracy, precision and validity
points.brief: Accurate results are close to the true value, precise results agree with each other, and valid results measure what was intended.

points.title: Repeatability and reproducibility
points.brief: Repeatable results come out the same when repeated; reproducible results come out the same with other people or methods.

points.title: Errors and limitations
points.brief: Random errors scatter results and systematic errors shift them one way. Every method has limits to report.
